prompt: You type `ip prefix-list MGMT seq 10 permit 192.0.2.0/24`, then `end`, and close the session. What happens at the router's next reboot?
hint: Where does the router read its configuration from when it boots?

choices.text: It is still there, because `end` saved it on the way out of configuration mode
choices.why: `end` only leaves configuration mode. Saving is a separate command.

choices.text: It is restored from the last backup
choices.why: Nothing in the router restores from a backup by itself; lesson 11 builds the backups.

choices.text: The prefix list is gone
choices.why: Right. Without `write memory` the change lived only in the running configuration, and a reboot loads the saved file.

choices.text: The router refuses to boot until someone confirms the change
choices.why: Routers boot from what was saved, confirmed or not.

prompt: On `edge1`, `ip prefix-list MGMT seq 10 permit 192.0.12.0/24` was accepted without an error. Why?
hint: What can a CLI check about a value?

choices.text: The router did not check the line, because configuration mode skips the checks
choices.why: It does check syntax: a malformed prefix is refused. This one was well formed.

choices.text: It is a valid network; the router cannot know it was meant to be 192.0.2.0/24
choices.why: Right. The syntax was fine and the intent was not the router's to know.

choices.text: FRR accepts anything and reports errors in its log
choices.why: FRR refuses malformed lines at the prompt, with a line starting with %.

choices.text: Prefix lists are not validated in FRR 8.4
choices.why: They are parsed like any other command; `192.0.12.0/24` simply parses.

prompt: In FRR, the command that copies the running configuration to the file the router boots from is `write ___`.
hint: It is typed at the `core1#` prompt.

prompt: The shell loop asked every router `show running-config | grep MGMT`. What did it find that three separate terminal sessions would have hidden?
hint: Look at the three answers side by side.

choices.text: That SSH was slow
choices.why: Nothing in the loop measured time.

choices.text: That `edge2` had rejected the command
choices.why: `edge2` was never sent the command; it was forgotten.

choices.text: That each router needed its own sequence number
choices.why: The same `seq 10` is correct on all three.

choices.text: That the routers disagreed: one right, one wrong, one missing
choices.why: Right. Each looked fine alone; asked the same question, they differed.

prompt: Match each thing that happened in the lab to the kind of manual failure it is.
hint: Three failures, three names.

pairs.right: A wrong value that is valid

pairs.left: Later changes start from three different routers

prompt: Why is "be more careful" not enough to fix manual changes on a large network?
hint: Think of a rate multiplied by something.

choices.text: It lowers the rate without reaching zero, and the rate is multiplied by devices and changes
choices.why: Right. A small rate times a large count is still a steady supply of mistakes.

choices.text: Careful people make more mistakes, because working slowly tires them out
choices.why: Nothing in the lesson says that; care lowers the rate.

choices.text: Routers reject changes typed slowly
choices.why: The CLI has no opinion about typing speed.

choices.text: Checklists are forbidden in change management
choices.why: They are common and useful; they just do not reach zero.

prompt: A script carries a typo in the line it sends. Compared with the same typo made by hand on one router, what is better about it?
hint: Where is the mistake, and how many places must be fixed?

choices.text: No advantage: a typo repeated on each router is strictly worse than a typo on one router
choices.why: It is worse in reach, better in how it is found and fixed.

choices.text: The router corrects typos that arrive from scripts
choices.why: The router cannot tell a script from a person.

choices.text: It lives in one file, is seen in the first router's output, and is fixed once
choices.why: Right. The mistake is everywhere, and it is also in one reviewable place.

choices.text: Netmiko refuses lines with typos
choices.why: Netmiko sends what it is given.

prompt: When routers that were meant to be configured alike slowly become different, one manual change at a time, the network is said to ___.
hint: The word the lesson uses for the third failure.

prompt: In `mgmt.py`, what does `save_config()` do on the lab's routers?
hint: It replaces a command you typed by hand.

choices.text: Closes the SSH session
choices.why: That is `disconnect()`.

choices.text: Downloads a copy of the configuration to `ctl`
choices.why: That would be a backup, lesson 11.

choices.text: Sends `write memory`
choices.why: Right. It is the save step for this driver.

choices.text: Checks that the prefix list is correct before sending it
choices.why: Nothing in `mgmt.py` checks the value.

prompt: After `mgmt.py` ran, `edge1` held one `MGMT` entry, not the typo plus the correct one. Why?
hint: Look at what the two lines had in common.

choices.text: The script deleted the prefix list first
choices.why: It sent only one line.

choices.text: Both used `seq 10`, and in FRR the sequence number identifies the entry
choices.why: Right. The new `seq 10` replaced the old one.

choices.text: FRR keeps the most recent line of a command and drops the rest, whatever the sequence number
choices.why: A different sequence number would have been added beside it.

choices.text: `save_config()` removes duplicates
choices.why: Saving copies what is running; it does not edit it.

prompt: Which of these were typed in one place in `mgmt.py`, instead of once per router? Choose all that apply.
hint: Look at the top of the file.

choices.text: The netops password
choices.why: There is no password in the file: it logs in with ana's key.

choices.text: The configuration line
choices.why: Yes, `LINE`.

choices.text: A different sequence number for each router
choices.why: It is `seq 10` everywhere.

choices.text: The list of routers
choices.why: Yes, `ROUTERS`.

prompt: The Netmiko method that enters configuration mode, sends a list of lines and leaves again is called ___.
hint: It is the line in `mgmt.py` that carries `LINE`.

prompt: At the lesson's assumed two minutes per router, how many hours does a change by hand on 300 routers take?
hint: Minutes first, then divide by 60.

prompt: `time python mgmt.py` printed `real 0m3.539s` for three routers. What does `real` measure?
hint: It is not what the processor did.

choices.text: Wall-clock time from start to prompt
choices.why: Right, and most of it was waiting for logins and prompts.

choices.text: Processor time spent inside Python
choices.why: That is closer to `user`.

choices.text: The time the routers took to save
choices.why: Saving is only part of it.

choices.text: The round trip to `core1`
choices.why: That is what `ping` measures.

prompt: Besides time, what else grows with the number of routers when a change is made by hand?
hint: Think about the first section of the lesson.

choices.text: The length of the configuration line
choices.why: The line is the same everywhere.

choices.text: The number of chances to make one of the three mistakes
choices.why: Right. Every session is another opportunity to mistype or forget.

choices.text: The cost of the router licences
choices.why: Unrelated to how the change is made.

choices.text: The time each SSH login takes
choices.why: Each login takes about the same time.

prompt: `mgmt_check.py` runs twice in a row on a network where nothing changed in between. What does the second run print?
hint: Look at the last capture of the section.

choices.text: `changed` for the router it fixed
choices.why: That router was fixed by the first run.

choices.text: An error, as the line exists
choices.why: The script checks first and does not send it.

choices.text: Nothing at all
choices.why: It reports every router either way.

choices.text: `already as intended` for every router
choices.why: Right. Nothing to do is the expected answer.

prompt: An operation that leaves the network the same whether it is applied once or twice is called ___.
hint: Ansible is built around this property.

prompt: Why is it worth checking before sending, when resending the same prefix-list line does no harm?
hint: Not every command is this harmless.

choices.text: Other commands reset sessions or add duplicates
choices.why: Right, and a script that asks first reports what it changed.

choices.text: Because FRR counts how many times a line was sent
choices.why: It does not.

choices.text: Sending costs money per command
choices.why: Not on any router in the lab.

choices.text: It makes the script faster on every router, since reading a configuration costs less than writing one
choices.why: It reads the configuration first, which is slower when a change is needed.

prompt: Somebody removed `MGMT` from `edge2` by hand. What is the first run of `mgmt_check.py` after that, in the language of this lesson?
hint: It found one difference and removed it.

choices.text: An omission
choices.why: The omission was the person's; the script found it.

choices.text: A rollback of the whole configuration
choices.why: It changed one line on one router.

choices.text: A correction of drift
choices.why: Right. The network had moved away from the intended state and was put back.

choices.text: A failed run, to be repeated later
choices.why: It printed `changed` and succeeded.

prompt: Put the four steps of a change in the order this course follows.
hint: The data comes first; reading back comes last.
trap: Validating after applying is the usual slip: by then the router has already seen the bad value.

prompt: `apply.py` refused `192.0.12.0/24`. Which router saw that value?
hint: Where does the check run?

choices.text: `core1` only
choices.why: The script stopped before the loop.

choices.text: All three, and each rejected it
choices.why: The routers would have accepted it, as `edge1` did.

choices.text: The first one in the list, then the script stopped
choices.why: No connection was opened.

choices.text: None
choices.why: Right. The check runs on `ctl`, before any connection.

prompt: The description is edited to `192.0.2.0/25`. What does `apply.py` do?
hint: Read the two checks exactly as written.

choices.text: Refuses it, as it refused `192.0.12.0/24`
choices.why: It is a valid network inside the management range, so both checks pass.

choices.text: Crashes, because /25 is not allowed in a prefix list
choices.why: Any prefix length is allowed.

choices.text: Applies it to the first router and then stops
choices.why: Nothing in the script stops midway on success.

choices.text: Applies it to all three routers
choices.why: Right. Validation catches only what somebody thought to check.

prompt: Why does `apply.py` end with a non-zero exit status when it refuses?
hint: Who reads an exit status?

choices.text: So the next program in a pipeline knows it failed
choices.why: Right. Lesson 14's pipeline stops on exactly that.

choices.text: To undo what it had applied
choices.why: It had applied nothing.

choices.text: Because `sys.exit` is how Python prints text
choices.why: It does print the message, but the status is the point.

choices.text: To make the routers reload their saved configuration
choices.why: Exit statuses stay on `ctl`.

prompt: Match each lab machine to what it is.
hint: The table in the section.

pairs.right: A device managed through its model

prompt: Which parts of the lab were written for this course rather than being existing open-source software? Choose all that apply.
hint: Three exceptions are named.

choices.text: The routers' REST API and gNMI port
choices.why: Yes, because FRR has neither.

choices.text: FRR's routing and CLI
choices.why: FRR is real.

choices.text: NetBox
choices.why: NetBox is real.

choices.text: The NAPALM driver for FRR
choices.why: Yes, because NAPALM ships none.

choices.text: The service desk
choices.why: Yes.

prompt: A script cannot reach `edge1`. Put the checks in the order the lesson gives.
hint: In the order the packets travel.

prompt: A colleague's script sends a change to 200 routers in sequence and prints nothing. What is the most useful thing to add first?
hint: What would you want to know after it ran?

choices.text: A line per router saying what it changed, read back from the router
choices.why: Right: verify, and report. Without it the run is not evidence of anything.

choices.text: Colours in the terminal
choices.why: Nice, but it says nothing about the network.

choices.text: A pause between routers
choices.why: It makes the run slower and no more informative.

choices.text: A second copy of the script for backup
choices.why: That protects the file, not the network.

prompt: Which of the three manual failures does `mgmt_check.py` detect on its own, without anyone telling it what happened?
hint: It compares each router with one wanted line.

choices.text: The typo on edge1, and not a missing line
choices.why: It also finds a missing line.

choices.text: The missing line on edge2, and not a wrong value
choices.why: A wrong value also fails the comparison.

choices.text: Any router that differs, whatever the cause
choices.why: Right. It does not need to know why a router differs.

choices.text: It sends without looking
choices.why: That was `mgmt.py`.

prompt: In the table of the scale section, how many minutes does a change by hand on 100 routers take in total?
hint: Two minutes each.

prompt: A change is described in a file, validated on `ctl` and applied, but nobody reads the routers back. Which failure can still ship unnoticed?
hint: The last box of the cycle.

choices.text: A typo in the description
choices.why: Validation is where that is caught, when a rule covers it.

choices.text: A router that refused or lost the change
choices.why: Right. Only reading back shows what the router really holds.

choices.text: A wrong list of routers in the description, so the change goes to the wrong devices
choices.why: That is a description error, reviewed before applying.

choices.text: A login that took longer than the others did
choices.why: Slowness is not a failure of the change.

prompt: What lets nine devices of the lab run on one Linux machine?
hint: Each device has its own interfaces, addresses and routes.

choices.text: Each is a network namespace, joined to the others by virtual cables
choices.why: Right. A namespace is a copy of the network stack, and veth pairs plugged into bridges are the cables.

choices.text: Each device is a small virtual machine of its own, started by the script
choices.why: Only the lab as a whole is a virtual machine; nine of them would need far more memory.

choices.text: Each device is a different port of one FRR process shared by all of them
choices.why: Each router runs its own FRR, inside its own namespace.

choices.text: The devices are only simulated, and no packet ever really travels between them
choices.why: The packets really travel between namespaces; only the hardware is missing.

prompt: Why does the course recommend a virtual machine over installing the lab on the computer you use every day?
hint: Think about what is left behind when you are done.

choices.text: What the lab installs stays installed, and a VM is deleted in one command
choices.why: Right. Routing software, a database and a switch are better kept in a machine you can throw away.

choices.text: The lab's commands work only inside a hypervisor, never on an installed Ubuntu
choices.why: They work on any Ubuntu 24.04, installed or rented.

choices.text: A virtual machine makes the three routers forward packets noticeably faster
choices.why: Speed has nothing to do with the choice.

choices.text: The transcripts match as printed only inside Multipass and nowhere else
choices.why: The table says all three paths match as printed.

prompt: You start a new lesson. What do you run first, and why?
hint: Every lesson's transcripts were made the same way.

choices.text: `sudo ~/netlab/netlab.sh reset`, to bring the routers back to how they boot
choices.why: Right. A change left on a router by the lesson before would show up in this one's output.

choices.text: `sudo ~/netlab/netlab.sh up`, because it rebuilds the whole lab every time it runs
choices.why: `up` does nothing to a lab that is already up; it says so and stops.

choices.text: Nothing at all: the routers forget every change the moment you leave `ctl`
choices.why: Leaving a shell changes nothing on the routers.

choices.text: Delete `ana`'s home directory, so the files from the last lesson are all gone
choices.why: Her home survives a reset on purpose, so your work stays.

prompt: After restarting the virtual machine, `sudo ~/netlab/netlab.sh enter ctl` answers `Cannot open network namespace "ctl"`. What happened?
hint: Where do network namespaces live?

choices.text: The namespaces lived in the kernel's memory and went with it; `up` rebuilds them
choices.why: Right. Nothing is broken, and `ana`'s files are still in her home.

choices.text: The restart deleted `netlab.sh` from disk, and it has to be saved all over again
choices.why: The script is a file on disk and survives a restart.

choices.text: The restart uninstalled FRR, so the `apt-get` line has to be run once more
choices.why: Packages survive a restart; only the namespaces are gone.

choices.text: `ctl` is renamed on every restart, and the new name is in the script's output
choices.why: The names are fixed in the script.

prompt: Running the script prints `/usr/bin/env: ‘bash\r’: No such file or directory`. What is wrong with it?
hint: Look at what follows `bash` in the message.

choices.text: It was saved with Windows line endings, a carriage return on every line
choices.why: Right. `file` says `with CRLF line terminators`, and `sed -i 's/\r$//'` takes the extra character off.

choices.text: bash is not installed on the virtual machine, and `apt-get` has to add it
choices.why: It is; the program being looked for is `bash` followed by a carriage return.

choices.text: The script was started without `sudo`, and the shell refused to find bash
choices.why: That gives `run it with sudo`.

choices.text: The virtual environment in `/opt/netauto` is missing, so nothing can start
choices.why: That has its own message, and the script never got that far.
